62:21.text: Then she let them down by a cord through the window: for her house was upon the town wall, and she dwelt upon the wall.

provenance.other: “by a cord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 2:15, and that verse is also the KJV's one instance of a cord, a wall and a letting-down in a single sentence. The New Testament has the manoeuvre twice more, both of Paul at Damascus: “let down by the wall” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:33, and Acts 9:25 has “let him down by the wall in a basket”. Neither of those has a cord. In the Book of Mormon “let down” occurs only at Alma 62:21 and 62:23, and “with a cord” only at 62:36 — three verses of one chapter, and nowhere else in the volume.
provenance.significance: Every biblical descent by cord over a city wall is an escape: Rahab's spies get out of Jericho, Michal's David gets out of the house, Paul gets out of Damascus. Alma 62 reverses the vector twice in seventeen verses. Moroni's men go down the wall to get *into* Nephihah, and Teancum goes down a wall on a cord to get into the Lamanite camp. The reversal is what makes the borrowing legible as more than a coincidence of siegecraft, and it is thematically exact: the manoeuvre that in scripture preserves a life is used here to take a city and, at 62:36, to kill a king and lose the killer. Note too what precedes it. Moroni goes up the wall by night “to spy out in what part of the city the Lamanites did camp”, which is Joshua 2:1's errand — men sent by night to spy out a walled city — and the cord follows the spying in Joshua as it follows it here. The city is taken “without the loss of one soul” (62:26), which is Jericho's outcome for Rahab's household and not for anyone else in it.

62:21.note: “They should prepare in haste strong cords and ladders, to be let down from the top of the wall into the inner part of the wall.” The nouns are ordinary and the combination is not: cord, wall, and a body let down over it is one KJV verse in the Old Testament and two in the New, and the Book of Mormon confines the whole vocabulary to this chapter. Filed as an allusion at moderate rather than high because siege narrative will independently produce ropes and walls, and because the Book of Mormon adds ladders, which no source has. What argues for dependence is the order of operations — night reconnaissance of a walled city, then a descent by cord — which is Joshua 2 in miniature and inverted.
62:21.whyNot: Ropes over walls are what armies actually use, and a writer describing an escalade needs no biblical model to reach for one. The strongest single string, “by a cord”, is at 62:36 and not here, and the Book of Mormon never uses the KJV's “let down by the wall”.

62:40.text: And the LORD said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.

provenance.other: “spare the place” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 18:24, and “spare all the place for their sakes” is its answer at 18:26; “fifty righteous” occurs in exactly three verses, all of them in this bargaining. “For the righteous' sake” in that exact form occurs in no KJV verse, which is why the catalogue filed the parallel at Alma 45:15 as insufficient-verbal — there was nothing there but the idea. Here the verb arrives with it: the Nephites “were spared”.
provenance.significance: Genesis 18 is the Bible's one sustained argument that a wicked city may be left standing on account of the righteous inside it, and the terms it settles on are exactly Mormon's: sparing, a place, and the righteous as the reason. What Mormon adds is the mechanism. Abraham's fifty righteous need only exist; Mormon's righteous pray — “because of the prayers of the righteous, they were spared” — which converts a bare arithmetic of merit into intercession, and thereby makes Abraham's own role in Genesis 18, the intercessor standing before the LORD, part of what is being borrowed rather than merely the frame around it. The verse closes a war narrative in which the Nephites have just executed everyone who would not fight; the sentence that spares them is the sentence God offered Sodom.

62:40.note: “There had been murders, and contentions, and dissensions, and all manner of iniquity among the people of Nephi; nevertheless, for the righteous' sake, yea, because of the prayers of the righteous, they were spared.” The catalogue declined this source at Alma 45:15 for want of any wording to test, and records that decision in the exclusion register; at 62:40 the wording is present — a people spared, for the sake of the righteous among them — and the sentence structure follows Genesis 18's own: the iniquity is stated first and at length, and the sparing is the concession that follows it. Held at moderate. The shared words are common, and only their configuration is rare.
62:40.whyNot: No string of any length is shared. “Spare”, “righteous” and “sake” are among the KJV's commonest religious vocabulary, and the doctrine that a land is preserved for the righteous within it is the Book of Mormon's own from 2 Nephi 1:7 onward and does not need Genesis to state it here.

62:50.text: And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:

provenance.other: Judges 8:34 is a fourteen-word verse and two of its phrases are KJV singletons: “remembered not the Lord their God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “delivered them out of the hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Both are in Alma 62:49-50, in Judges' order, with the negative removed. Separately, “how great things” at the head of 62:50 belongs to a five-verse KJV family (1 Samuel 12:24, Mark 5:19, Mark 5:20, Luke 8:39, Acts 9:16); the Book of Mormon's “the Lord had done for them” has Mark's divine title rather than Samuel's “he” or Luke's “God”, which is the form already adjudicated at 1 Nephi 7:11 and 2 Nephi 1:1 and is listed here as a composite rather than given a second row.
provenance.significance: Judges 8:34 is the epitaph on Gideon's generation — the sentence with which the book of Judges announces that deliverance did not take. Alma 62:49-50 is the epitaph on the war chapters, and it is Judges 8:34 read backwards clause for clause. “Remembered not the Lord their God” becomes “neither were they slow to remember the Lord their God”; “delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies” becomes “he had delivered them out of the hands of their enemies”. Mormon is writing the notice that Judges refused to write. The metalepsis costs him something, because a reader who recovers Judges 8:34 also recovers what stands on either side of it — 8:33, where Israel goes a-whoring after Baalim “as soon as Gideon was dead”, and 9:1, where Abimelech makes himself king over Shechem and murders his brothers. Alma 62:52 records that Helaman died; Helaman 1 opens with a contention over the judgment seat and a political murder. The borrowed verse carries its own sequel, and the sequel arrives on schedule.

62:50.note: “Neither were they slow to remember the Lord their God … yea, they did remember how great things the Lord had done for them … and he had delivered them out of the hands of their enemies.” Two KJV singletons out of one fourteen-word verse, in the source's order, with the source's polarity reversed. This is the strongest link in Alma 62 and the machine stream found it: Judges 8:34 scored an eight-word run at this verse. The reversal is the whole interest — the Book of Mormon takes the Old Testament's flattest statement that Israel forgot its deliverer and uses it, negated, as its own certificate of a people who did not.
